Dutch Government Plans to Phase Out 25,000 Civil Servant Roles, Relying on AI to Save Billions

Overview of the Dutch Workforce Overhaul

The Dutch government has announced a sweeping structural initiative to reduce its central government workforce by approximately 25,000 positions over the coming years. Facing a record-high number of approximately 160,000 central government employees—which represents a 41% surge since 2018—officials are turning to artificial intelligence and automation to absorb daily workloads and boost overall productivity by 20%.

The initiative aims to achieve recurring financial savings of €900 million annually by 2027, scaling up to €3.5 billion (approximately $3.9 billion) each year starting in 2035. Eric van den Burg, the State Secretary for Effective Government, stated that the administration is prepared to make difficult choices to establish a simpler, smaller system.

Implementation Strategy and Structural Changes

To bridge the gap left by reduced human staffing, the cabinet plans to present a detailed strategy early next year outlining how artificial intelligence will be deployed across operations. When current employees depart their roles, agencies will evaluate whether a machine or AI tool can handle the tasks before authorizing a human replacement.

The broader modernization effort encompasses several administrative and physical adjustments:

  • IT Standardization: Consolidating and standardizing technology systems across distinct government departments to minimize technical clutter.
  • Office Space Reduction: Introducing a "one desk for every two employees" policy alongside the sale of surplus government real estate.
  • Regulatory Trim: Simplifying or eliminating at least 500 administrative rules annually to cut red tape.

Exemptions and Scope of Reductions

While policy-making agencies and general ministries face significant shrinkage—with certain departments projected to experience workforce reductions between 45% and 60%—critical public sectors are shielded from the plan. The police and defense forces are strictly protected from these job cuts.

Although the Netherlands maintains a relatively low budget deficit of 1.8% compared to many European Union peers, long-term fiscal conservatism has driven the administration to pursue structural reform ahead of compounding financial pressures.

Practical Implications and Reader Verification

For public sector workers, contractors, and observers tracking European public administration trends, this policy marks a notable shift toward automating civil service duties.

  • Confirmed Facts: The central government workforce currently stands at roughly 160,000 employees. The plan targets a reduction of 25,000 jobs, aims for €3.5 billion in annual savings by 2035, and protects police and defense personnel.
  • Unknowns and Uncertainties: Exact departmental breakdowns, the specific software architecture, and the precise timeline for individual ministry rollouts remain pending until the detailed cabinet plan is released early next year.
